inline.s: [Essential Explanation] To believe in principle is to deeply believe that the hundred thousand koṭi of lands in truth do not lie outside this present, momentary single thought-mind of mine, because this present single thought-nature of mine truly has nothing outside it. It is also to deeply believe that the subjective and objective worlds, the main and accompanying figures, of the West are all reflections appearing within my present single thought-mind. The whole of phenomena is the principle; the whole of delusion is truth; the whole of practice is the nature; the whole of other is self. Because my mind is all-pervasive, the Buddha’s mind is also all-pervasive, and the mind-nature of all beings is all-pervasive. It is like a thousand lamps in a single room, each light interpenetrating the others, mutually interwoven again and again, without hindrance. This is called believing in principle.

[Note] To believe in principle is to deeply believe that the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss is manifested within my present, momentary single thought-mind. “The subjective and objective worlds, the main and accompanying figures” generally refers to everything in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

[The momentary single thought-mind] The single thought-mind of the present instant. “Jie’er” describes what is exceedingly minute and tiny: “Jie” means weak or small, and “er” is a particle. [The subjective and objective worlds, main and accompanying figures] Here “the objective world” (the dependent reward) refers to the four lands of the Land of Ultimate Bliss (the land of common beings and sages dwelling together, the land of expedient liberation with remainder, the land of the real reward, and the land of eternal tranquility and light); “the subjective world” (the primary reward) refers to Amitābha Buddha and the beings there; “the main” is Amitābha Buddha, and “the accompanying” are the beings there (bodhisattvas, voice-hearers, human beings, and gods). [The whole of phenomena is the principle, the whole of delusion is truth, the whole of practice is the nature, the whole of other is self] Here “whole” (quan) means thoroughgoing. When one is truly thoroughgoing, one realizes that phenomena and principle are non-dual, delusion and truth are non-dual, nature and practice are non-dual, and self and other are non-dual; and one can the more realize that mind and land are non-dual.

[Essential Explanation] Having believed thus, then this Saha world is the defiled realm that one’s own mind has evinced, and since one’s own mind is defiled, one should rightly be wearied of it and seek to leave it. The Land of Ultimate Bliss is the pure realm that one’s own mind has evinced, and since one’s own mind is pure, one should rightly aspire to it and seek it. Wearying of the defiled, one must renounce it to the utmost, only then has one nothing more to renounce. Aspiring to the pure, one must grasp it to the utmost, only then has one nothing more to grasp. Therefore the Miaozong says: If grasping and renouncing are carried to the utmost, they are not a different path from neither grasping nor renouncing. If one does not engage in the matter of grasping and renouncing, but only esteems neither grasping nor renouncing, that is to cling to principle and discard phenomena. Having discarded phenomena, principle too is not complete. If one realizes that the whole of phenomena is principle, then grasping is also principle, and renouncing is also principle. Each act of grasping and each act of renouncing is wholly the Dharma-realm. Therefore, after believing, one must understand the vow.

[Note] Once deep faith is established, an earnest vow arises: to be wearied of the Saha world and to seek the Land of Ultimate Bliss. This wearying and seeking (the mind’s leaving the defiled and seeking the pure) should be undertaken on the level of phenomena; one must not cling to principle and discard phenomena.

[The Miaozong] The Miaozong Chao, the Excellent Purport Commentary on the Contemplation Sūtra of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life, composed by the Venerable Siming of the Song dynasty, is abbreviated as the Miaozong Chao.

[Essential Explanation] As for the practice of holding to the name with single-minded, undisturbed concentration: the name summons the virtue (of the Buddha), and that virtue is inconceivable, so the name itself is inconceivable. Because the merit of the name is inconceivable, even scattered recitation becomes a seed of Buddhahood, and holding to the name attains the stage of non-retrogression. The various sūtras set forth the practices of the Pure Land as manifold and diverse—such as contemplating the image, contemplating the features, bowing and making offerings, the five repentances and six recollections, and so on. When each of these practices is fulfilled, one is reborn in the Pure Land. But the single method of holding the name gathers in the widest range of beings and is the easiest to put into practice. Therefore the compassionate Blessed One Śākyamuni, without being asked, proclaimed it himself, singling it out for the wise Śāriputra. It may be called the foremost expedient among expedients, the unsurpassed ultimate meaning among ultimate meanings, the most perfectly sudden among the perfectly sudden. Hence it is said: cast a pure pearl into turbid water, and the turbid water cannot but become clear; cast the Buddha’s name into a confused mind, and the confused mind cannot but become Buddha.

[Note] The practitioner holds to the name with single-minded, undisturbed concentration. The practices of the Pure Land are manifold and diverse, yet the single method of holding the name gathers in the widest range of beings and is the easiest to put into practice. It may be called the foremost expedient among expedients, the unsurpassed ultimate meaning among ultimate meanings, the most perfectly sudden among the perfectly sudden.

[Scattered recitation becomes a seed of Buddhahood; holding to the name attains non-retrogression] This is a common elliptical construction in the classical text, referring back to the preceding passage, with the meaning: scattered recitation of the name is still a seed of Buddhahood, while one who holds to the name with single-minded, undisturbed concentration is reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss and directly attains the stage of non-retrogression. [The five repentances] The Tiantai Master Zhiyi, for those cultivating the Lotus samādhi, set down five methods of repentance: first, repentance—laying open one’s past offenses and admonishing oneself for the future; second, entreaty—entreating the Buddhas of the ten directions to turn the wheel of Dharma; third, rejoicing—rejoicing in and praising all roots of goodness of self and other; fourth, dedication—directing the merit one has cultivated toward beings and the Buddha Way; fifth, making vows—making the four great vows to guide the preceding four practices. [The six recollections] Recollection of the Buddha, recollection of the Dharma, recollection of the Saṅgha, recollection of the precepts, recollection of giving, recollection of the heavens.

[Essential Explanation] Faith, vows, and holding to the name constitute the true cause of the One Vehicle; the four Pure Lands constitute the wonderful fruit of the One Vehicle. When the cause is raised, the fruit must follow, and so faith, vows, and holding to the name are the proper theme of this sūtra. The characteristics of the four Pure Lands are set forth in detail in the Miaozong Chao and in the Profound Meaning of the Brahma Net Sūtra; here they are not fully recounted. They will be briefly indicated later in the explanation of the main text.

[Note] Once more it is pointed out that faith, vows, and holding to the name with single-minded, undisturbed concentration are the proper theme of this sūtra. One should give particular attention to the fact that in this section Master Ouyi has already given a clear definition of faith, vows, and practice: faith means believing in oneself, believing in another, believing in the cause, believing in the fruit, believing in matters, and believing in principle; vow means being wearied of the Saha world and seeking the Land of Ultimate Bliss; practice means holding to the name with single-minded, undisturbed concentration. Therefore, whenever the following text speaks of “faith,” it means believing in oneself, believing in another, believing in the cause, believing in the fruit, believing in matters, and believing in principle; when it speaks of “vow,” it means being wearied of the Saha world and seeking the Land of Ultimate Bliss; when it speaks of “practice,” “holding the name,” or “holding to,” it means holding to the name with single-minded, undisturbed concentration.

[The four Pure Lands] Also called the four Buddha-lands or the four lands, namely, the land of common beings and sages dwelling together, the land of expedient liberation with remainder, the land of the real reward, and the land of eternal tranquility and light. The land of common beings and sages dwelling together is the land where ordinary beings and sages who manifest in the world to teach beings dwell together; the land of expedient liberation with remainder is the land where the two vehicles and bodhisattvas who have not yet realized the Dharma-body dwell; the land of the real reward is the land where the Buddha’s reward-body and the bodhisattvas on the grounds dwell; the land of eternal tranquility and light is the land manifested by the Buddha’s pure Dharma-body.

Concerning the three bodies and the four lands, Master Xing’an (Sheng’an) explains in his Commentary on the Text on the Western Pure Land: “Q: There is only one Western Land, so why divide it into four lands? And there is only one Buddha, so why are there three bodies? Is this not a tearing apart and dividing? A: It is like a single moon, which yet has different light and shadow; and like a single mirror, which yet has different images and brightness. How have the light and shadow been torn apart, or the images and brightness of the mirror been divided? The Dharma-body is like the moon, the reward-body like the light, and the manifestation-body like the shadow. The land of eternal tranquility and light is like the mirror’s substance, the land of the real reward like the mirror’s light, and the lands of expedient liberation and of common beings and sages dwelling together like the mirror’s images. As for the Buddha, it is the single Dharma-nature body that dwells in the land of eternal tranquility and light. For the bodhisattvas of the ten grounds and the thirty minds (the ten abidings, ten practices, and ten dedications, called the thirty minds), he manifests the complete reward-body and dwells in the land of the real reward. For voice-hearers and bodhisattvas, he manifests the superior and inferior bodies and dwells in the land of expedient liberation. For ordinary beings and the bodhisattvas of first resolve, he manifests the inferior response-body and dwells in the land of common beings and sages dwelling together.”

[The superior and inferior bodies] The superior response-body and the inferior response-body. The Tiantai school divides the Buddha’s response-body into two kinds, superior and inferior; the superior is called the superior response-body, the body manifested in response to the bodhisattvas of the first ground and above. The inferior is called the inferior response-body, such as the sixteen-foot Buddha-body the Buddha manifests for ordinary beings before the grounds and for those of the two vehicles. [Before the grounds] Before the first ground. Those before the grounds are bodhisattvas at the level of ordinary beings; only upon reaching the grounds are they bodhisattvas of the Dharma-body.
[Essential Explanation] Fourth, clarify the function and power. This sūtra takes rebirth and non-retrogression as its function and power.

[Note] “On the function” discusses, from the theme, the power and function (the effect) of a sūtra. This sūtra takes rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss and directly ascending to the stage of non-retrogression as its function and power. The sūtra says: “The beings born in the land of the Land of Ultimate Bliss are all avaivartika (non-retrogressive).”

[Avaivartika] Rendered in Chinese as “non-retrogression.” It means that merit and roots of goodness increase ever more without loss or regression, up to the attainment of Buddhahood. Ordinarily, a bodhisattva must pass through a great aeon (a mahākalpa) of cultivation before reaching this stage of non-retrogression.

[Essential Explanation] Rebirth is in four lands, in each of which nine grades are distinguished. Let me briefly set forth the characteristics of being born in the four lands: if one holds to the name but has not cut off the delusions of views and thought, then according to whether one is scattered or concentrated, one is divided into three grades and nine classes within the land of common beings and sages dwelling together; if one holds to the name until reaching single-mindedness in mundane matters, so that the delusions of views and thought fall away spontaneously, then one is born in the Pure Land of expedient liberation with remainder; if one reaches single-mindedness in principle, suddenly breaking through one degree of ignorance, and even up to forty-one degrees, then one is born in the Pure Land of the real reward, and also partially realizes the land of eternal tranquility and light; if ignorance is entirely cut off, then it is the highest real reward and the ultimate state of eternal tranquility and light.

[Note] [In each, nine grades are distinguished] In the land of common beings and sages dwelling together, nine grades are distinguished according to the heaviness or lightness of the delusions of views and thought; in the land of expedient liberation with remainder, nine grades are distinguished according to the heaviness or lightness of the delusions of dust-and-sand; in the land of the real reward and the land of eternal tranquility and light, nine grades are distinguished according to the heaviness or lightness of the delusion of ignorance. [According to whether scattered or concentrated] Here “scattered” means that although one has not reached concentration in reciting the Buddha’s name, one has already reached the point where deluded thoughts, once they arise, are not continued. [The three delusions] The delusion of views and thought, the delusion of dust-and-sand, and the delusion of ignorance. The delusion of views is the confusion and error of ordinary beings in their views—such as the five wrong views of the view of self, the view of extremes, the perverted view, the view of self-assertion, and the view of attachment to precepts and practices. The delusion of thought is the confusion and error of ordinary beings in their thoughts—such as the afflictions of greed, hatred, delusion, pride, and doubt. These two delusions are the root of beings’ wandering in the three realms and vainly undergoing birth and death; cutting them off, one can end birth and death and escape the three realms. The delusion of dust-and-sand is the delusion of the bodhisattva; if a bodhisattva, in saving beings, does not penetrate the countless Dharma-gates as numerous as dust and sand, he cannot complete the task of teaching beings, and so it is called the delusion of dust-and-sand. The delusion of ignorance is the fundamental ignorance, which can obstruct the principle of the true reality of the Middle Way; when it is entirely cut off, one becomes a Buddha. Among the three delusions, views and thought are coarse, dust-and-sand is intermediate, and ignorance is subtle.

[Essential Explanation] Non-retrogression has four meanings. First, non-retrogression of thought: breaking ignorance, revealing the Buddha-nature, directly born in the land of the real reward, and partially realizing the land of eternal tranquility and light. Second, non-retrogression of practice: once the delusions of views and thought have fallen away and the delusion of dust-and-sand is also broken, one is born in the land of expedient liberation and advances toward the ultimate fruit. Third, non-retrogression of position: carrying karma, one is reborn in the land of common beings and sages dwelling together; born from the womb of the lotus, one is forever free of conditions of regression. Fourth, ultimate non-retrogression: regardless of whether one recites with utmost sincerity or with a scattered mind, whether with a concentrated or an absent mind, whether one understands or not, yet the name of Amitābha Buddha, or the names of the Buddhas of the six directions, or the name of this sūtra, once they enter the ear—though a thousand myriads of kalpas pass—will ultimately lead to liberation by virtue of this. It is like hearing the poisoned drum: near and far, all are struck down; and like eating a small piece of vajra: it is certain never to be digested.

[Note] Non-retrogression has four meanings. First, non-retrogression of thought: thought after thought flows into the ocean of the Tathāgata’s fruit, breaking ignorance, revealing the Buddha-nature, and directly being born in the land of the real reward, and also partially realizing the land of eternal tranquility and light. Second, non-retrogression of practice: once the delusions of views and thought have been cut off and the delusion of dust-and-sand is also broken, one is born in the land of expedient liberation, constantly practicing the practice of saving beings and seeking upward the Buddha Way. Third, non-retrogression of position: carrying karma, one is reborn in the land of common beings and sages dwelling together; born by transformation from the lotus, one is forever free of conditions of falling back. Fourth, ultimate non-retrogression: whether one recites with utmost sincerity or with a scattered mind, whether with a concentrated or an absent mind, or whether one understands the meaning or not, so long as the name of Amitābha Buddha, or the names of the Buddhas of the six directions, or the name of this sūtra (the Amitābha Buddha Sūtra), once passes through the ear, it is stored in the alaya consciousness as a seed of Buddhahood, never to be destroyed. Though a thousand myriads of kalpas pass, when the roots of goodness mature, one will ultimately be liberated by this. The universality of liberation upon hearing the name is like hearing the sound of the poisoned drum, upon which the greed, hatred, and delusion of near and far all die out; and the seed of Buddhahood, once heard, endures without destruction, like taking a small amount of vajra, which is certain not to vanish with the passage of time.

[The poisoned drum] This drum is coated with a poisonous substance, so that one who hears its sound dies at once. The Chan school uses it as a metaphor for the pointed words of a master that cause a student to extinguish greed, hatred, and delusion. Master Quanhuo said: “My teaching is like the poisoned drum: strike it once, and those who hear it, near and far, are all struck down.” (from the Record of the Transmission of the Lamp)

[Essential Explanation] Furthermore, those who, carrying karma, are born in the land of common beings and sages dwelling together in purity and realize the non-retrogression of position all dwell together with the buddha-to-be (the successor bodhisattvas)
(all like the successor bodhisattvas who hold the position to succeed the Buddha)
, and are likewise all, in a single lifetime, certain to fill the Buddha’s position
(all are to become Buddhas in a single lifetime).

Now, to dwell together in one place with the superior good is to be born in the land of common beings and sages, and already to be born horizontally into the three higher lands; to fill the Buddha’s position in one lifetime is the non-retrogression of position, and already to perfectly realize the three non-retrogressions. Such function and power have never been had among a thousand sūtras and ten thousand treatises. Compared with those who, suddenly awakening to the true cause, merely ascend the steps out of the world, and who, only after being non-retrogressive from life to life, can hope for the stage of Buddhahood—these cannot be spoken of on the same day. How could those of the doctrinal and Chan schools fail to reflect on this?
[Those of the doctrinal and Chan schools] Here “zongjiao” refers to the Chan school (the school of the patriarchs) and the doctrinal school (the scriptural schools).

[Essential Explanation] Fifth, the teaching’s characteristics. This sūtra is included in the great-vehicle Bodhisattva Piṭaka. It is also the Dharma spoken without being asked, sustained by the loving-kindness and compassion of utmost great love, able to cause beings of the final Dharma age, so obstructed and hindered, to rely upon it and directly reach non-retrogression. Therefore, when the Dharma and its teachings are to be extinguished in the future, this sūtra will be especially kept in the world for a hundred years, to widely deliver sentient beings. It is the agada medicine that governs all diseases, absolutely perfect and interfused, inconceivable. The profound treasury of the Avataṃsaka, the secret marrow of the Lotus, the essential purport of all Buddhas, the compass of the ten thousand practices of the bodhisattvas—none of these go beyond it. Should one wish to praise and recount it widely, even a whole kalpa would not suffice; the wise will know this for themselves.

[Note] The teaching’s characteristics of this sūtra are included in the great-vehicle Bodhisattva Piṭaka; it is the profound treasury of the Avataṃsaka, the secret marrow of the Lotus, the essential purport of all Buddhas, and the compass of the ten thousand practices of the bodhisattvas.

[Classification of teachings] To distinguish the greater and lesser, and the provisional and real, of the doctrines. [Bodhisattva Piṭaka] The general name for the great-vehicle scriptures, so called because they contain the methods by which great-vehicle bodhisattvas cultivate the cause and realize the fruit. [Included] The Buddha, with compassionate teaching, gathers in and embraces beings. [Beings] Also called sentient beings—all living things possessed of consciousness. [Sentient] One who possesses a conscious mind, that is, a sentient being. [The agada medicine] Also called the medicine of deathlessness. This medicine is wondrous, of immeasurable value, and when taken, can universally remove all diseases. [The compass] An instrument used in ancient China to discern direction, equivalent to the modern compass.

blocks.text: 1. The Holy Assembly of the Dharma Gathering

inline.s: [Essential Explanation] Entering the text, it is divided into three parts: first, the introductory part; second, the main part; and third, the part that spreads the teaching. These three are called the beginning good, the middle good, and the end good. The introduction is like the head, in which the five sense organs are all present. The main part is like the body, in which the internal organs are without defect. The part that spreads the teaching is like the hands and feet, which move without obstruction. Therefore, when the Master Zhiyi explained the Lotus Sūtra, he treated the first chapter entirely as the introduction, and the latter eleven and a half chapters as the spreading of the teaching. Again, in the two gates of the traces and the essential, each is divided into three sections. Thus the five chapters beginning with “the Dharma-teacher” are all the spreading of the trace-gate. For the introduction must always draw the thread of the whole sūtra, and the spreading of the teaching prevents the gift of Dharma from being dammed up; the significance is not small. Later people, not understanding this, see where the text touches upon doctrinal principle and at once judge it to belong to the main part, reducing the introduction and the spreading of the teaching to mere conventions. How can they still be called the beginning also good and the end also good!
[Note]

The scripture is divided into three main parts: first, the introductory part; second, the main part; and third, the part that spreads the teaching. The introductory part recounts the circumstances that occasioned this sūtra. The main part is the main teaching of this sūtra. The part that spreads the teaching lists the benefits of upholding this sūtra and urges one to uphold, recite, and spread it. Here Master Ouyi emphasizes that one must not slight the introductory part and the part that spreads the teaching.

[The Master Zhiyi] His name was Zhiyi, and he is the first patriarch of the Tiantai school. This school takes the Lotus Sūtra, the Nirvāṇa Sūtra, the Great Perfection of Wisdom Sūtra, and the Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom as its principal works, and sets forth the wonderful principle of the three contemplations in a single mind. [One time] The Tiantai Commentary on the Contemplation Sūtra says: “Here, without discussing the length or brevity, whether provisional or real, when the preaching of this sūtra is finished, it is all called ‘one time.’” [The two gates of the traces and the essential] The gate of the essential (the original) and the gate of the traces (the manifest), abbreviated as the essential gate and the trace gate. This was established by the Tiantai Master Zhiyi, and later commentators on the Lotus Sūtra have without exception divided it into the essential gate and the trace gate. “Essential” refers to the original ground accomplished in the long-distant past; “traces” refers to the manifest traces freshly accomplished. The essential gate refers to the original ground on which the Tathāgata achieved the Way in the far-distant past; the trace gate refers to the Buddha newly manifested, who, to teach beings, responds with manifest traces.
